THOUGHT: The patient is an 11-year-old girl with a classic prodrome of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and headache one week prior, followed by a facial rash that spares the perioral area (a “slapped-cheek” appearance—though not explicitly named, the perioral sparing is highly characteristic), and then progression to a lacy, reticular, mildly pruritic rash on the trunk and extremities. This temporal sequence—prodromal viral illness → facial erythema with circumoral pallor → lacy reticular rash on body—is pathognomonic for erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), caused by parvovirus B19. The age group (school-aged child), absence of systemic toxicity (normal vitals except mild fever), normal CBC except for slightly elevated platelets (a nonspecific finding; parvovirus B19 can cause transient reticulocytopenia but platelet count is typically normal—mild elevation may reflect mild inflammation or be incidental), negative strep throat culture (ruling out scarlet fever), and lack of other concerning features (no arthralgias—less common in children, no purpura, no respiratory distress, no lymphadenopathy) further support this. Other considerations—e.g., measles (would have cough/conjunctivitis/Koplik spots, more toxic appearance), rubella (postauricular/occipital adenopathy, milder rash but not typically lacy), drug eruption (no medication history), or enteroviral exanthem—are less consistent with the classic triphasic pattern and distribution. The lacy reticular pattern is distinctive for parvovirus B19.

DIAGNOSIS: Erythema infectiosum
